body_markdown:
Jenny Simpson, one of the most accomplished American middle-distance runners of her generation, has announced her retirement from competitive athletics after doctors diagnosed her with a rare heart condition following a cardiac arrest during a race in June.


The 39-year-old former world champion revealed that she has been diagnosed with **Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC)** , a condition affecting the heart muscle that can cause abnormal and potentially dangerous heart rhythms. Simpson said the diagnosis means returning to competitive running would put her health at serious risk.


Her announcement brings an emotional end to a remarkable career that included a world championship title, an Olympic medal and years of success at the highest level of international athletics.


## A Sudden Collapse Changed Everything


Simpson's career took an unexpected turn in June when she collapsed while taking part in a mile run in Raleigh, North Carolina.


Rather than competing in a major championship race, Simpson was helping to pace a group of young girls during the event. She suddenly went into cardiac arrest on the track, requiring immediate emergency treatment.


Medical responders performed CPR, while an automated external defibrillator was also used before Simpson was transported to hospital for further care.


The speed of the response proved crucial. In a statement shared after the incident, the Sir Walter Running Team expressed its gratitude to the people who responded immediately, as well as emergency medical services and healthcare professionals who treated Simpson.


The incident could easily have had a devastating outcome. Instead, Simpson survived and was eventually able to share her diagnosis and future plans publicly.


## Simpson Reveals Her Diagnosis


In an Instagram statement, Simpson explained that her cardiac arrest was linked to ARVC.


The condition can interfere with the normal electrical activity of the heart and may lead to dangerous heart rhythms. For an elite athlete whose career depends on intense physical exertion, such a diagnosis can fundamentally change what is considered safe.


Simpson said the diagnosis had made it clear that she could not return to competitive running.


She described her decision as the end of one chapter of her life, while also emphasising that surviving the cardiac arrest had given her a different perspective on what comes next.


Her message was notably positive despite the seriousness of the circumstances. Rather than wanting sympathy, Simpson asked people to focus on the fact that she survived.


She encouraged those around her to tell her that they were glad she was still here.


That response reflects the perspective of an athlete who understands that her sporting career is only one part of her identity.


## A Career Defined by Major Achievements


Simpson leaves competitive running with an impressive record.


For much of the period beginning in 2007, she established herself as one of the leading American female 1,500-metre runners. Her consistency at international level helped make her one of the defining middle-distance athletes of her era.


One of the biggest moments of her career came at the **2011 World Championships** , where she won the world title in the 1,500 metres.


That victory confirmed Simpson's place among the best middle-distance runners in the world.


She also reached the podium at the World Championships on two other occasions, finishing runner-up twice. Her international achievements were complemented by Olympic success.


At the **2016 Rio Olympics** , Simpson won bronze in the 1,500 metres, adding an Olympic medal to her collection of major honours.


Her career therefore ends with the distinction of being both a world champion and an Olympic medallist.


## Why the Retirement Decision Matters


For elite athletes, retirement can be an emotional decision under normal circumstances. Simpson's situation is considerably different because her decision has been influenced by a potentially serious medical diagnosis.


Athletes train for years to push their bodies to extraordinary levels. Giving up competition after reaching the top of the sport can therefore be difficult, particularly when the decision is not entirely voluntary.


However, Simpson's circumstances demonstrate why health has to come before sporting ambition.


ARVC can cause potentially dangerous abnormalities in heart rhythm, meaning intense exercise may carry significant risks for people with the condition. For Simpson, continuing to compete would therefore not simply be a question of whether she could maintain her previous performance levels.


It would involve a fundamental question about personal safety.


Her decision to step away from competition highlights the importance of listening to medical advice, particularly when symptoms or diagnoses involve the heart.


## From Champion Athlete to a New Chapter


Although Simpson's competitive career has ended, her influence on athletics is unlikely to disappear.


She leaves behind a legacy that extends beyond medals and championship results. Her career represents years of dedication to middle-distance running and a sustained presence on the international stage.


Her decision to speak openly about what happened may also help raise awareness of serious cardiac conditions that can affect athletes.


Cardiac events during exercise are uncommon, but Simpson's experience demonstrates why emergency preparedness at sporting events matters. The availability of trained responders, CPR and defibrillation can be critical when someone suffers a cardiac arrest.


The June incident also serves as a reminder that even highly trained athletes can experience unexpected medical emergencies.


## Looking Beyond the Track


Simpson's retirement is undoubtedly the end of a significant sporting era for the American runner, but her own words suggest that she does not view it as the end of her story.


After surviving a life-threatening event, she appears determined to focus on what remains possible rather than only on what she can no longer do.


That perspective makes her retirement announcement particularly powerful.


Athletes are often defined by their results: championship victories, records, medals and performances. Simpson's career contains all of those achievements, but her next chapter may be defined by something different — resilience.


At 39, she leaves the sport as a world champion and Olympic medallist, but she also leaves with something more important: the opportunity to continue living beyond the finish line.


Her competitive running career may have reached its conclusion, but Jenny Simpson's story clearly has not.


Source: **The Independent** on 21 August 2026.
